headline: New Hampshire opens $1 million grant program for chargers at tourism destinations
dek: The new program will reimburse up to 80% of eligible costs for public Level 2 chargers at places such as ski areas, parks and downtown districts, with the first application window closing Nov. 15.
body: New Hampshire is offering about $1 million to help build public electric-vehicle charging stations at places that draw visitors, a move state officials say can support both tourism and cleaner transportation. The Recharge the Adventure New Hampshire program focuses on travel- and tourism-oriented locations rather than limiting awards to government property. The New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services and Department of Business and Economic Affairs announced the program Tuesday, according to the [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://newhampshirebulletin.com/2026/10/06/nh-announces-1m-program-to-boost-spotty-ev-charger-network/).

The eligible settings are broad enough to reach communities across the state: parks, ski areas, beaches, downtown districts and other attractions can apply if a proposed project meets the program requirements. Public agencies, private organizations and nonprofits are eligible applicants. That structure gives municipalities and regional destinations a path to add charging where visitors already stop, while also allowing privately operated tourism businesses to participate.

The grant is designed as a partial reimbursement. It can cover as much as 80% of eligible project costs, up to $10,000 for each Level 2 charging port, according to the [Southern New Hampshire Planning Commission’s program notice](https://www.snhpc.org/m/newsflash/home/detail/30). Applicants will have to finance the work initially and seek reimbursement under the grant agreement. The program also sets a $100,000 cap for projects within any one municipality, although the published program information says the state may consider exceeding that cap for a compelling project or one with substantial public or economic benefits.

The state is also reserving at least $40,000 for each of New Hampshire’s nine regional planning commission areas. The geographic set-aside matters because charging availability is uneven: the Bulletin reported that a February 2025 analysis by Clean Energy New Hampshire and Ski New Hampshire counted 597 charging ports in the state, the lowest total among New England states in that report. The analysis said New Hampshire represented about 5% of the region’s charging infrastructure and linked the shortage to lost tourism dollars.

The money comes from New Hampshire’s Volkswagen Environmental Mitigation Trust, which holds settlement funds from Volkswagen’s Clean Air Act case. Using that source ties the new awards to air-quality goals while directing part of the money toward a practical barrier for electric-vehicle travelers. Level 2 chargers are slower than highway fast chargers, but they are suited to places where visitors may remain for an hour, an afternoon or an overnight stay. A charger at a trailhead, town center or ski-area property can therefore serve a different purpose from a short highway stop.

The application process is rolling rather than built around one single deadline. The first monthly window closes Nov. 15, and later applications will be considered until the available funding is committed, according to the regional planning commission notice. A webinar for prospective applicants is scheduled for Oct. 14. Applicants will need to show that their sites are publicly accessible and that the proposed equipment and location fit the program’s tourism and transportation goals.

For New Hampshire communities, the program offers a relatively modest but targeted way to improve the visitor experience before winter travel and the next tourism seasons. It does not create a statewide fast-charging network, guarantee an award to every applicant or resolve the larger question of how quickly charging infrastructure should expand. It does give destinations a chance to add ports with state-backed cost sharing, and it spreads a portion of the funding across every regional planning commission area.

The next important steps are the Oct. 14 applicant webinar and the Nov. 15 first submission window. Until awards are announced, the number and locations of new chargers remain unknown. State officials’ stated goal is to make it easier for electric-vehicle drivers to explore New Hampshire while helping local businesses and communities capture spending from those visitors.
author: NorthEast News Desk
